html:
The Tacana are an Indigenous people of the northern Bolivian lowlands, living in the forests along the Beni and Madre de Dios rivers. About 5,000 people are Tacana, and some 1,800 still speak the Tacana language, of the Tacanan family.

They farm, hunt and fish, and gather Brazil nuts. Franciscan missionaries founded mission towns among them, such as Tumupasa and Ixiamas. In the 1800s outsiders came for cinchona bark, which gives quinine, and then for rubber in the rubber boom, and many Tacana were made to work for them.

Their kin include the Ese Ejja and the Araona. Part of their land lies in Madidi National Park, and they hold a large community territory in Bolivia.
